lesson.menu_desc: A debtor, a divorce and a house that changed owners just before the lawsuit: explaining what had happened before the case started -- He had already transferred... -- 35 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 5 -- The House in Her Name
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Ana Caroline Teixeira Nomiyama | Lesson 5 -- The House in Her Name
lesson.grammar_point: past perfect: had + past participle for the action that happened FIRST, before another past action (By the time we filed, he had already transferred the house); already / before / by the time / when

listenings.text: A few years ago, I represented a group of creditors against a businessman in London. He owed them more than five million pounds. When the trial started, we looked for his assets, and we found nothing. He had transferred his yacht and his apartment to his brother six months before. The brother had paid almost nothing. That was our first red flag. We investigated the dates, the prices and the bank accounts. In the end, the court decided that the transfers were fraud against the creditors. It voided them, and the assets went back to pay the debts. It took two years, but it worked.

When I investigate a debtor, I always look for three red flags. The first is the person. Was the property transferred to a family member, an ex-spouse or a close friend, just before the lawsuit? The second is the price. Nobody sells a house for ten dollars. And the third is control. Does the debtor still live in the house, or still use the money? In one case, a man told the court that he had nothing. But we found out that he had opened a new bank account in his mother's name, and he was still using the card every day. One red flag is a question. Three red flags are a story.

I'm a family lawyer, so I see this from the other side. Creditors sometimes think that every divorce is a trick to hide money. But most divorces are real. People separate for real reasons, and they divide the property. Last year, a bank tried to void my client's divorce settlement. She had kept the family house. But she had separated from her husband two years before his company had any problems. We showed the court messages, her new apartment and three witnesses. The judge agreed that the divorce was real. The timing is important, but it's not the only fact. You have to look at the whole story.
